entry.title: Naming batch 55: animation channel slots, input devices, drawable parsing
entry.summary: One hundred fifty consecutive functions across animation channels, DirectInput handling, model drawables, JPEG codec glue and graphics setup are now named, with six left explicitly unnamed where the purpose could not be determined.
entry.content:
One hundred fifty consecutive functions across animation channels, DirectInput handling, model drawables, JPEG codec glue and graphics setup are now named, with six left explicitly unnamed where the purpose could not be determined.

What was asked

Propose descriptive names for a batch of unnamed game functions, working out what each address group is about first and grading every name with a confidence.

What was found

Verified The animation channel classes share one vtable layout whose slots now have meanings: object deletion, cloning, per-type sampling at a frame time, an adopt-or-compress slot, an allocation-size slot and a resource serializer. Static channels compress by uniformity check, curve channels by recursive least-squares fitting, run-length channels by rice encoding.

Verified The keyboard and mouse initializers are pinned by their DirectInput device identifiers, the gamepad path by its XInput library strings, and a control-map save and load pair by a four-letter stream magic.

Verified The drawable section parsers are pinned by their keywords: version header, skeleton, joint limits, bounding center and radius. One frustum test calls the named frustum helper.

Verified Six JPEG glue functions are the standard image-library source and destination callbacks, recognized by the fake end-of-image marker written on stream exhaustion and by the five-callback install shape.

Verified Three symbol-table entries labelled as fragment-drawable deleting destructors are actually multiple-inheritance thunks that adjust the object pointer and call into the draw workers.

What was decided or recommended

Naming lanes should read the actual virtual tables rather than trusting slot labels, check sibling lanes for per-family vocabulary before inventing names, and treat any deleting-destructor label as guilty until the disassembly shows a free. The stream read and write helpers are now pinned by direction, which future serializer lanes can rely on.

How to reproduce it

All evidence was gathered with mapped-image reads and a linear disassembler: per-function tables of calls, imports, string references and data references, verified-rewrite doc comments for sibling slots, virtual-table dumps, and direct reads of the short functions. The batch evidence table and full disassembly stay in the lane scratch folder.

What was confusing or went wrong

One batch entry spans four entry points (a draw slot plus three co-located thunks), so it is named for its primary slot with the sharing noted. Two composite fan-out functions call a slot on every child drawable but no evidence says to what end, so they are unnamed rather than guessed. A six-byte jump into the encrypted code prefix is likewise unnamed.

entry.title: A callee that pops more than its call site pushes
entry.summary: Verifying a batch of ped-task functions turned up a case every lane should check for: a helper that pops five words while its call site pushes only two, because three floating-point arguments are stored above the stack pointer before the pushes. The checker cannot catch a wrong argument count here, so I verified all 35 callees in the batch independently.
entry.content:
Verifying a batch of ped-task functions turned up a case every lane should check for: a helper that pops five words while its call site pushes only two, because three floating-point arguments are stored above the stack pointer before the pushes. The checker cannot catch a wrong argument count here, so I verified all 35 callees in the batch independently.

What was asked

Rewrite eight neighbouring task-system functions and prove each rewrite identical to the original, including the largest one, a 780-byte updater with fifteen callees and five global tables.

What was found

Verified All eight functions verified at 1200 trials each with every mutant caught.

Verified One helper pops five words where its call site pushes two. The remaining three arguments are constant floats stored before the pushes, so the declaration genuinely has five parameters and the rewrite must push all five. A nearby stack read only makes sense with the five-word cleanup: with two it would read a caller-saved register instead of the intended table index.

Verified The checker's call stubs pop the argument count from the contract on both sides, so a wrong count is invisible to every check while silently moving the post-call stack. Any function whose code reads stack slots after a stubbed call needs its callees' true cleanups confirmed outside the checker.

What was decided or recommended

All 35 direct callees in the batch had their true cleanup sizes decoded by following control flow from each entry to its returns, and every one matches its contract. Lanes should run the same audit wherever post-call code reads stack-relative slots: count pushes at the call site is not enough, because arguments can be pre-stored.

How to reproduce it

Decode each callee recursively from its entry, collecting every reachable return and its pop count, and compare with the contract's argument count. Separately, inspect each call site for stores to outgoing stack slots above the pre-push stack pointer. Where the two disagree, the callee's epilogue wins and the contract must declare the full count.

What was confusing or went wrong

The tail index first looked like an incoming callee-saved register, which no worker transport can deliver to a rewrite and which would have made the function unverifiable. Three hand stack traces agreed on that reading before the epilogue decode showed the five-word cleanup and settled it as a plain local. A linear sweep had also suggested a wrong pop count for one small helper; the control-flow decode corrected it.

entry.title: Naming the animation channel region: slot table, cache slots, compressor
entry.summary: One hundred fifty consecutive animation functions were all named, most at high confidence, by decoding the channel vtable slots once and reusing them everywhere, and by scanning for callers to pin down four cache entry points.
entry.content:
One hundred fifty consecutive animation functions were all named, most at high confidence, by decoding the channel vtable slots once and reusing them everywhere, and by scanning for callers to pin down four cache entry points.

What was asked

Propose descriptive names for a batch of one hundred fifty unnamed game functions, working out what the group is about first, with a confidence per name.

What was found

Verified The batch is one animation region in five groups: tolerance and channel-group lifecycle, channel base and raw channel methods, a mutex-guarded animation cache, creature mover and skeleton components, and channel bit tools with the remaining channel subclasses.

Verified The channel vtable slots are consistent across eleven subclasses: destructor, heap clone, per-type frame samplers, per-type indexed samplers, a double-returning float evaluator, per-type try-build-from-samples returning success, storage size, and serialize. The base indexed samplers just convert the index to a frame and tail-call the frame sampler.

Verified Track compression picks the smallest encoding that succeeds: the float picker tries static, delta, quantized and raw builds, and the integer worker tries three integer builds the same way. Vector and quaternion tracks first try a static collapse, then per-component float builds or raw keys depending on version.

Verified Four near-identical cache find-or-create functions serve different users: degree-of-freedom data, float channels, animation tracks, and the dispatch path, with nine, three, nine and thirteen callers respectively.

Inferred A further channel type id seen in the integer picker belongs to a run-length-encoded integer channel class referenced by nearby callers.

What was decided or recommended

Later naming lanes covering channel subclasses should reuse this slot table instead of re-deriving it, and should run a caller scan before reading big functions: caller names decided the merge, clone, rebase and cache names here. The inventory subsystem labels split this region into three; all of it is animation code.

How to reproduce it

Disassemble through the mapped image with the standard toolchain, diff same-size neighbours to find family parameters, read verified rewrite doc comments for functions already rewritten in range, and byte-scan nearby clean code for direct calls into the batch to attribute callers.

What was confusing or went wrong

Early helper lookups returned garbage disassembly until it became clear the callees sit in the encrypted first megabyte of code; behaviours depending on them were named from the readable side only. One batch entry overlaps the following functions because its recorded size counts padding, so disassembly extents were checked by hand there.

entry.title: Naming a run of animation frame and creature functions
entry.summary: One hundred fifty consecutive unnamed functions turned out to be almost entirely the animation frame system, and the inventory labels for a third of them were wrong. All 150 are now named except two bare-constant virtuals.
entry.content:
One hundred fifty consecutive unnamed functions turned out to be almost entirely the animation frame system, and the inventory labels for a third of them were wrong. All 150 are now named except two bare-constant virtuals.

What was asked

Propose a descriptive name for each function in the batch, with a confidence and one sentence of evidence, working out what the group is about first.

What was found

Verified The batch is the frame degree-of-freedom machinery (create, find, insert, sort, copy, blend, dispatch) plus creature components, filters, tolerances and two id registries.

Verified Every dispatcher in the batch shares one shape: try a mutex-guarded fetch, run the masked kernel on success, the gated kernel on failure, the direct kernel with no context.

Inferred The functions the inventory calls audio in this range are animation track blending: they use the same key bytes, skip flag and quat-or-vector-or-float dispatch as the animation kernels, and an audio mixer would not twist quaternions. Three verified audio names and the audio tag here look like misnomers; behaviour verified, nouns suspect.

Verified The component registry maps kind ids to descriptors holding factory pointers, and two batch factories are its BlendShapes and ExtraDofs entries.

What was decided or recommended

  • Named 148 of 150 (36 high, 112 medium); two constant-returning tolerance virtuals left empty with low confidence.
  • Subsystem set to animation throughout, against the inventory tags, with the audio conflict flagged for the coordinator rather than silently followed.
  • Next naming lane should clip disassembly at the next known entry: two inventory sizes in this batch swallow their neighbours.

How to reproduce it

Read the executable through the mapped image, disassemble each batch entry, and tabulate direct calls, import calls, string immediates and callers before naming anything. Resolve callee names against the merged symbols, lane names and verified index; confirm classes through the c-animation vtable records; diff near-identical neighbours instead of reading each twice. Scripts and tables are kept in the lane scratch folder.

What was confusing or went wrong

Two inventory sizes overlap their neighbours, which first produced phantom callees; the true bodies are short factories jumping to constructors that appear in no list. A raw byte scan for callers produced false positives from call opcodes inside other instructions. Several callees sit in the encrypted range and decode as garbage, which caps the confidence of everything depending on them. The largest functions were head-read only for lack of time.

entry.title: A task lookup that passes its own return address to a callee
entry.summary: One ped task-management routine reads the word above its own stack frame, which is its return address, and hands it to a helper as an ordinary argument. The helper only checks whether the low byte is zero, and every known caller returns to an address with a nonzero low byte, so in practice the helper always takes the same path. The rewrite passes a constant with a nonzero low byte instead, and the proof records the one skipped argument openly.
entry.content:
One ped task-management routine reads the word above its own stack frame, which is its return address, and hands it to a helper as an ordinary argument. The helper only checks whether the low byte is zero, and every known caller returns to an address with a nonzero low byte, so in practice the helper always takes the same path. The rewrite passes a constant with a nonzero low byte instead, and the proof records the one skipped argument openly.

What was asked

Rewrite five neighbouring task-management routines in Rust and prove each one behaves identically to the original with the differential checker.

What was found

  • Verified The find-or-attach routine has three stages plus a random sweep, ten callees at eleven call sites, and no global state of its own.
  • Verified On its final sweep path it loads a word from above its own stack frame and passes it as the second argument of the attach helper. Hand simulation of the stack pointer along every path to that read shows the slot always holds the return address.
  • Verified The helper reads only the low byte of that argument and only tests it for zero; its body was read in full and the byte is never used as a value.
  • Verified The routine has exactly four direct callers in the program, and all four return to addresses with nonzero low bytes, so the shipped game always takes the helper's nonzero path here.
  • Inferred The most likely source-level cause is an uninitialised variable or a wrong stack slot in the original code, but the machine behaviour is deterministic: each caller gets its own fixed value.

What was decided or recommended

The rewrite passes a constant with a nonzero low byte at that site, which takes the same helper path under the stated precondition, and the contract skips only that argument at only that site while comparing every other argument of every other call. The rewrite's documentation states the precondition and the divergence if a future caller ever returned to a zero-low-byte address. A narrow proof that says so was judged acceptable; a variant that silently passed zero would always take the helper's other path and was rejected as genuinely divergent.

How to reproduce it

Disassemble the find-or-attach routine and simulate the stack pointer from the entry along the path through the three missed stages to the sweep loop: the value moved into the callee-saved register before the final helper call comes from the return-address slot. Then read the helper's body and note the three loads of its second argument's low byte feeding two zero-tests and nothing else. Finally, scan the program's code for direct calls to the routine and check the low byte of each address following a call.

What was confusing or went wrong

The first reading of the routine's stack frame was off by confusion between decimal and hexadecimal offsets and briefly suggested the routine read uninitialised scratch; careful re-simulation in hex showed the slot is exactly the return address on every path. Two contracts also failed first contact for ordinary reasons: a global address with a bad subtraction, caught by the undeclared-write check naming the right address, and a set of code addresses missing a digit, which the worker refused as not call sites.

entry.title: Naming a tokenizer, math, steam and animation batch: slot correspondence and shared bytes
entry.summary: One hundred and fifty consecutive functions were named with 146 names, and the most reusable finding is a naming signal: the ascii and binary tokenizer classes share one vtable layout, so a width measured on the binary side names an otherwise identical ascii writer. Two corrections came out of the same batch: a widely used string helper folds case, and several math cores carry script-native names they do not deserve.
entry.content:
One hundred and fifty consecutive functions were named with 146 names, and the most reusable finding is a naming signal: the ascii and binary tokenizer classes share one vtable layout, so a width measured on the binary side names an otherwise identical ascii writer. Two corrections came out of the same batch: a widely used string helper folds case, and several math cores carry script-native names they do not deserve.

What was asked

Propose descriptive names for 150 consecutive unnamed functions spanning file tokenizers, quaternion and angle math, the steam client, indexed file slots, animation evaluation and loading, a mini heap allocator, and frame degrees of freedom. No rewriting, only names with confidence and one sentence of evidence each.

What was found

Verified The ascii and binary tokenizer vtables share slot meanings. Seven read slots and four write slots were checked independently on both sides and agree, so the three byte-identical ascii integer writers take their widths from the one, two and four byte binary writers in the same slots.

Verified The string compare helper used by the token-name checks folds upper case to lower case before comparing. It is a case-insensitive compare, and the named-read wrappers therefore verify token names case-insensitively.

Verified The steam callback registration uses callback id 331, and the tracked vtable name for the callback struct identifies the event as the overlay-activated event, so the id needed no guesswork.

Inferred Several shared math cores carry script-native names from the native that happened to call them (sine, cosine, arccosine, floating modulo). Their call shapes and constants match the plain math identities, and later lanes should treat the native names as labels of callers, not of the functions.

Verified Identical code folding shares bytes across unrelated classes: one small float getter serves dozens of classes, and paired readers differ only in staging versus direct store with identical results. Nine names in this batch intentionally cover two or three addresses each, each saying so in its evidence.

GroupFunctionsNamed
Ascii and binary tokenizers4040
Color, quaternion, angle and compression math2222
Steam client and async file io99
Indexed file slots1915
Animation and frame degrees of freedom6060

What was decided or recommended

  • When two implementations share a vtable interface, measure widths and arities on the side where they are visible and transfer them; record the transfer in the evidence sentence.
  • When two addresses hold behaviorally identical bytes, give both the same honest name and note the duplication rather than inventing a distinction.
  • Leave unconditional return-true stubs unnamed with low confidence; four were left empty here because the bytes cannot show their role.
  • Five large animation bodies were sampled rather than read fully and their names carry that caveat; they are the natural targets if this batch is revisited.

How to reproduce it

Build one evidence table for the whole batch first: disassembly plus referenced strings, imports, resolved call targets, constants and floating point flags per function. Decode one function with a verified rewrite end to end before trusting the address mapping. Then decode the small plain callees just outside the batch (the typed readers behind the wrappers, the case-folding worker, the allocator and vtable owners in the tracked structure files) and read the batch against them. Keep the names file current every twenty-five functions.

What was confusing or went wrong

The named-read wrappers call a string compare and discard the result, which looked like dead code until the sixth identical instance made the compiled-out assert the only sane explanation. One write slot breaks the slot correspondence (sixteen bytes where a three-float vector was expected); it is flagged, not forced. Early in the batch the string helper was assumed to be case-sensitive compare from its shape, and only decoding its worker corrected that. Nothing else went wrong; the batch finished with time to spare because the table answered most questions before individual reads began.

entry.title: Naming 150 particle, shader, tree, time and tokenizer functions
entry.summary: One hundred thirty-six of the batch got descriptive names, and the register functions turned out to be the best naming signal in the project so far: each one spells out its class name, size, factory and load hooks in a fixed layout.
entry.content:
One hundred thirty-six of the batch got descriptive names, and the register functions turned out to be the best naming signal in the project so far: each one spells out its class name, size, factory and load hooks in a fixed layout.

What was asked

Propose a descriptive name with confidence for each of 150 consecutive game functions, working out what the group is about first. Only names, no rewriting.

What was found

Verified The batch holds eight groups: particle event emitter and effect virtuals with their constructors and destructors, particle property-list registers and XML parsers, the full shader-variable family of eight subtypes, a complete red-black tree implementation, the game time manager, two 4x4 matrix inverses, a name dictionary, and the text tokenizer with twenty virtuals.

Verified Seventeen register functions share one descriptor layout: class name, class size, factory function and named load hooks. Reading that layout resolved every factory, every class size and three load hooks without guessing.

Verified Virtual slot 15 returns the type name and slot 16 the class descriptor in every vtable checked, across particle and shader classes alike.

Verified One inventory entry is not a function: it starts mid-function at a branch target, falls back into its owner, then holds padding and the next function head.

Inferred Six tokenizer virtuals are behaviorally identical duplicates of siblings, down to the same helper calls; they were left unnamed with pointers to their twins rather than given invented distinctions.

What was decided or recommended

Names follow prior-lane conventions: class double-colon method for virtuals and constructors, register and create prefixes for descriptor and factory functions, and empty names with low confidence where no evidence distinguishes a purpose. The next naming lane should dump the register table and the vtables for the whole binary once, since those two sources resolve entire function families, and byte-compare same-size neighbors before reading each one. Two possible conflicts were flagged for the coordinator: a neighboring lane's constructor claim spanning many of these register functions, and a shared tree-erase name claimed at two addresses.

How to reproduce it

Read the executable through the mapped image, never the raw file at a mapped address. Build one evidence table per function with referenced strings, called imports, named callees and vtable slots, then disassemble only the short functions and the unclear ones. Confirm each factory by matching its installed vtable against already-named per-type methods, and confirm each register function by its name string, size constant and installed factory.

What was confusing or went wrong

The binary spells one class name with an extra infix that an earlier string read had silently dropped; only the raw bytes settled it. A whole family of functions showed zero direct callers until it became clear their addresses are installed into runtime descriptors rather than called. The first evidence export was unreadable because the shell redirect wrote it in a wide encoding, so later scripts wrote their own files directly.

entry.title: A flag test that means the opposite of what it says
entry.summary: While rewriting a camera follow function, a three-instruction floating point gate turned out to test for nonzero rather than for not-a-number, and the checker caught the misreading on the first run.
entry.content:
While rewriting a camera follow function, a three-instruction floating point gate turned out to test for nonzero rather than for not-a-number, and the checker caught the misreading on the first run.

What was asked

Rewrite two neighbouring camera functions in Rust and prove each behaves identically to the original with the project checker, which runs both sides from identical state and compares results, memory, and outgoing calls.

What was found

Verified The smaller function blends two vectors by a countdown-driven factor. Its blend gate compares three values against zero and jumps on the processor parity flag after masking the comparison result. Reading the jump as "taken when unordered" is wrong: the jump checks the parity of the masked value, and that parity is even for greater-than, less-than, and unordered alike. Only an exactly-equal result falls through. So the gate runs the blend when any value is nonzero, with not-a-number counting as nonzero.

Verified The larger function reuses the same idiom three times, plus a fourth comparison whose skip branch is dead: the flag bit it tests is cleared two instructions earlier with no call in between, so the guarded path can never run. Its rewrite keeps the branch for fidelity.

Verified The same larger function copies a scratch word from its own uninitialised stack into both output vectors. The checker gives both sides identical stack fills, so the proof pins that word to zero and says so.

What was decided or recommended

The small function is verified. The large one is verified through its early-return path; its full contract is written and validated, and the rewrite continues in the next lane. Any lane meeting a compare, flag-load, mask-test, conditional-jump sequence should work out the parity table by hand instead of trusting the jump mnemonic.

How to reproduce it

Run the lane's contracts with the stock checker: the small function passes over a thousand trials with float results compared bit-exactly, and its deliberately wrong version (one countdown update skipped) fails as required. The stage contract for the large function passes the same way on its covered path.

What was confusing or went wrong

The first attempt at the small function failed a third of its trials because the gate was transcribed as a not-a-number test. The mismatch pointed straight at the blend decision, and writing out the four parity cases by hand showed the error. A similar mislabeling of one scratch slot in the large function survived its stage proof unnoticed because nothing on the covered path observes that slot; it is recorded as an erratum for the next stage.

entry.title: Naming session tasks and particle keyframes
entry.summary: One hundred forty-five of one hundred fifty consecutive functions were named, and the session-task virtual slots now have plain meanings: start, polled update, finish, descriptor getter.
entry.content:
One hundred forty-five of one hundred fifty consecutive functions were named, and the session-task virtual slots now have plain meanings: start, polled update, finish, descriptor getter.

What was asked

Propose descriptive names for a batch of one hundred fifty unnamed functions that form two natural groups: multiplayer session-task code with its message codec, and the particle keyframe and timeline system.

What was found

Verified The session-task interface uses five slots with consistent behaviour: one marks the task started, one advances it each tick, one completes it and notifies, one returns a static descriptor, and one matches gamers. The event classes expose their id through a single stub each.

Verified Pack and parse routines are told apart by which encrypted helpers they call: writers use one pair plus a bit writer, readers use a result-pair reader plus a different helper.

Verified The particle side holds struct-class registrations, class-descriptor getters, keyframe array primitives with slope computation, keyframe load and save hooks, and timeline methods that fan out per phase over emitters, including a camera-distance-sorted dispatch.

Inferred Two large message handlers belong to the session-migration task: their field offsets only fit that task's size, and they have no direct callers, matching runtime-dispatched handlers.

What was decided or recommended

Names follow the conventions earlier lanes set for registrations, descriptor getters, event ids and message pack and parse routines. Five functions were left unnamed rather than guessed: two generic allocators, two timeline fan-outs whose phase is unknown, and one emitter predicate bit. The next naming lane should run a whole-binary caller scan first, read class names from runtime type records where structure lanes have no entry, and keep the same conventions.

How to reproduce it

Disassemble each function from the mapped executable image, resolve its callees through verified rewrites and lane names, join vtable slots against the structure files, scan the binary for callers and data references, and read class names from the runtime type records beside each vtable. Two inventory entries need care: one records a size that truncates its function, and one entry point sits inside another function and shares its tail.

What was confusing or went wrong

The bitstream and allocator helpers live in the encrypted part of the binary and cannot be read, so message identity had to come from caller context at most two hops away. One shared slot implementation serves two classes, and was filed under the class whose code region holds it. A first attempt at inline shell scripting failed on quoting, so every script was written to a file instead.

entry.title: Two verified, an uninitialised stack read, and a vector-argument gap
entry.summary: Verified A production batch of eight neighbouring pedestrian-task functions yielded two verified Rust rewrites, and two findings worth keeping: one verified function copies a stack slot it never wrote into three words of a matrix it hands to a callee, and another function cannot be verified at all because a callee takes its arguments in two full vector registers while the checker can only transport 32 bits of each.
entry.content:
Verified A production batch of eight neighbouring pedestrian-task functions yielded two verified Rust rewrites, and two findings worth keeping: one verified function copies a stack slot it never wrote into three words of a matrix it hands to a callee, and another function cannot be verified at all because a callee takes its arguments in two full vector registers while the checker can only transport 32 bits of each.

What was asked

Rewrite eight neighbouring pedestrian-task functions in Rust and prove each rewrite identical to the original with the differential checker, which runs both sides from identical state and compares return values, memory, stack adjustment, outgoing calls and faults over at least one thousand trials each, with a deliberately wrong version per function to show the contract can tell right from wrong.

What was found

  • Verified A leaf classifier that maps one input byte to 1 or 0 over a set of 108 values verified cleanly on the first attempt with every input value covered several times.
  • Verified A six-call setup routine verified with three disclosed narrowings: one callee pops fewer words than the caller pushed so only the top word is compared, the snapshot covers 8 of the 16 matrix words, and the stack fill is fixed to zero.
  • Verified The setup routine reads a frame slot it never wrote and copies it into three matrix words. Tracing every stack-pointer-relative store shows no write to that slot before the three reads; with the checker's stack fill fixed to zero the original reads zero there, matching a rewrite that uses literal zeros. In a real run those words carry stale stack content. Whether any callee observes them is unknown.
  • Verified A task virtual function defers on a proven checker gap: one of its paths calls a helper with no stack arguments whose inputs arrive as a double plus residue in one vector register and two doubles in another. The checker's register transports move one 32-bit word each and the comparison then checks all four words, so no contract can observe those arguments; reading the checker's own stub generator confirms the 32-bit move.
  • Inferred Four deferred functions form one family sharing the same callees, including one that pops fewer words than pushed and one entered with no stack arguments at all. They are verifiable in principle but each needs a full stack-pointer trace first, because pushes between stores shift every frame offset and some stores overlap.

What was decided or recommended

  • Verify the four-function family together in a later lane, since one analysis of the shared callees serves all four; the lane report holds the per-callee retry plan.
  • A full-vector argument transport (four stack words per register) would unlock the deferred virtual function; until then it stays deferred rather than narrowed, because the blind path holds half its behaviour.
  • Contracts that declare fewer compared words than a callee receives should generate the uncompared constants from the disassembly by script, as was done here, so a typo cannot slip into the blind spot.

How to reproduce it

Copy the checker driver into lane scratch space, build a small rewrite crate for the 32-bit target depending on the checker runtime by path, and write one contract per function declaring the callee scripts, heap objects with a planted virtual table for the indirect call, the one global dword, and the fixed stack fill. Run the driver once per contract with at least one thousand trials; each contract also runs its wrong version, which must fail. The lane's generator scripts assert every constant in the contracts against the executable's mapped bytes before emitting them.

What was confusing or went wrong

The first attempt at the setup routine went vacuous: both sides faulted identically at the indirect call because the contract linked the fabricated object to the wrong heap segment. A single-trial debug script printing the fault address and the resolved request words found it in minutes. Later, a rebuild failed twice with the output file locked by an unknown process; no worker held it by module scan, so the crate was rebuilt into a fresh target subdirectory under the same lane folder with the crate name unchanged.

entry.title: Naming a particle and shader batch: slots, registrars and false friends
entry.summary: One hundred fifty consecutive functions across the particle system, the fragment heap, procedural textures, shader lighting classes and session networking were named 142 to 8, and the most reliable signals were vtable slot reads, a repeated class-registrar shape, and preload callback ordering.
entry.content:
One hundred fifty consecutive functions across the particle system, the fragment heap, procedural textures, shader lighting classes and session networking were named 142 to 8, and the most reliable signals were vtable slot reads, a repeated class-registrar shape, and preload callback ordering.

What was asked

Propose descriptive names for a consecutive run of unnamed functions, working out what the group is about first, with a confidence per name and no rewriting.

What was found

Verified Sibling classes repeat one virtual interface: the same slots hold the per-frame update, a shader-variable test, a variable-cache factory and a class getter, each with an identical small size, so one solved sibling names the rest.

Verified Class registration has a fixed shape: a singleton-guarded builder storing a descriptor and chaining base-class builders, with preload and postload callbacks pushed in string order. Reading which callback sits under which string names the parser and finalizer directly.

Verified Reading vtable slots from the mapped image identifies constructors, destructors and factories without disassembling them: each stores or references its class table, and slot zero of each table points back at the deleting destructor.

Inferred The effect-rule class embeds six keyframe members, not three as an earlier layout lane reported; both its constructors and one virtual method iterate all six.

What was decided or recommended

Follow the sibling-slot wording exactly where shape and slot agree, use the register, preload and postload vocabulary already established by neighbouring lanes, and number parallel algorithm channels rather than inventing semantics for them. Leave forwarders to unnamed slots and context-free allocators empty.

How to reproduce it

Build one evidence table per batch first: referenced strings, imports, internal callees with merged names, and caller sites resolved to enclosing functions through the full inventory. Disassemble small functions fully, large ones by head and tail, and cap every decode at the next inventory start. Check any zlib-looking string by scanning for who pushes it before believing it.

What was confusing or went wrong

Verified The first evidence script indexed the mapped image by file offset and produced garbage; the mandated known-function decode check caught it at once. A text-search tool silently returned nothing on files a plain script search matched, so all searching moved to scripts. One instruction that looked like a zlib string use turned out to be a flag-byte check, and no readable code pushes those strings at all.

entry.title: Naming 150 functions: water, chat, fragments and particles
entry.summary: One batch of 150 unnamed functions turned out to be four subsystems in a row: procedural water and sky textures, multiplayer text chat plus a sibling peer table, fragment parsing with its event and dictionary helpers, and particle effect loading. All but one function got a name, about two thirds of them at high confidence.
entry.content:
One batch of 150 unnamed functions turned out to be four subsystems in a row: procedural water and sky textures, multiplayer text chat plus a sibling peer table, fragment parsing with its event and dictionary helpers, and particle effect loading. All but one function got a name, about two thirds of them at high confidence.

What was asked

Name each function in the batch with a descriptive name and a confidence, using strings, imports, known callers and class layouts as evidence, without rewriting anything.

What was found

Verified The opening group builds and renders procedural water and sky: setup, resource creation, per-frame update and render virtuals, a reflection constructor, noise-texture slot setters whose exact textures fell out of the sky initialisation path, and a small shader-variable registry.

Verified The middle group is multiplayer text chat: registration, serialisation and sending for the text and typing-indicator messages, plus a full peer manager (init, start, stop, add, clear, find, receive, update). A second manager shares the same framework but has smaller payload-less entries and inline bitstream sync; its domain stayed unknown, so its names stay structural.

Verified The fragment group parses child definitions field by field. Each parser's identity came from the field registry, which records group, field and handler together: masses, bone index, four event blocks, animations, bone tags, locators, bounds and skeleton references. Supporting pieces include event-set copy and place routines, a binary-search name dictionary with dictionary place support, and bound loaders driven by a type factory.

Verified The closing group loads particle effects: chunk loading, four rule-dictionary loaders with per-element constructors, dictionary destructors, effect removal from three global lists, quad-vertex emission and keyframe teardown.

Verified Three techniques carried the batch: walking runtime type records to name every vtable touched, reading field-registry call sites to get group-field-handler triples for parsers, and mapping callers to already-named neighbours to place each function.

What was decided or recommended

  • Next naming lanes should walk the type records first when a batch touches vtables; it settles class questions in minutes.
  • Parser batches should be read through their registry call sites rather than function by function; the pushed field names identify each handler exactly.
  • String evidence must be checked for pointer use: one function matched a compression error string only because a flag byte sat at a nearby address, and it is really a particle vertex writer.
  • Caller scans miss everything in the encrypted low region of the executable, so a function with no visible caller is usually driven from there, not dead.

How to reproduce it

Read code through the mapped image rather than the raw file, decode one known function end to end to confirm the mapping, then gather per-function evidence (referenced strings, imported calls, call targets, caller names from merged symbols and lane names, data references to the batch) into one table before reading bodies. Resolve vtables through their type records and parser handlers through their registry triples, then read the short and unclear functions fully.

What was confusing or went wrong

Two blind alleys cost time. The particle vertex writer looked like a decompressor because of the false string match above; only reading the body showed pure floating-point record emission. The message descriptor blocks looked like ordinary vtables but mix code pointers with data, so slot-based guessing about the chat messages was dropped in favour of behaviour evidence. One function, a plain jump to a shared drawable routine whose callees are all encrypted, was left unnamed at low confidence rather than guessed.

entry.title: Naming the particle system batch: class descriptors, keyframe idioms and folded vfuncs
entry.summary: A batch of one hundred and fifty consecutive functions turned out to be the whole particle effects subsystem, and one repeated code shape unlocked most of it.
entry.content:
A batch of one hundred and fifty consecutive functions turned out to be the whole particle effects subsystem, and one repeated code shape unlocked most of it.

What was asked

Name each function in a consecutive unnamed batch, working out what the group is about first, with a confidence per name.

What was found

Verified The batch is the particle system: emission domains in four shapes, standard emit rules with keyframed emitter data, and render-side shader variables and templates. The inventory cluster labels pointed elsewhere and were ignored.

Verified Ten functions share one registration shape: an init-once guard, an allocation, then a filled class descriptor holding the class name string, instance size, create callback and parent descriptor, registered with a factory. Each descriptor create slot points at that class factory function, which made factories trivial to confirm.

Verified The last slot of every vtable in the batch just returns its class descriptor global, matching the naming precedent other lanes set for a different subsystem. The deleting destructors all share one identical sixteen-instruction body.

Verified One keyframe sampling loop shape recurs across about fifteen functions: walk fixed-size entries comparing entry time, then slope-interpolate. Recognising it once made the domain evaluators, the emit-rule track samplers and the simulation kernels all readable.

Verified The linker folded identical bodies across unrelated classes: one float setter serves a shader variable slot and two physics-node slots, and one bare return instruction serves vehicle and emit-rule slots. Shared bodies need one name with a note, not one name per class.

What was decided or recommended

Names follow existing lane precedent for constructors, deleting destructors, class registration and class getters. Behaviour-clear but wording-mine names got medium confidence; six pure getters and setters of unknown fields and one opaque render setup were left empty at low confidence. The next naming lane in this area should name the small shared callees first: the keyframe init and destroy family, the dictionary find and add pair, and the path, open, parse and close file helpers, since about thirty medium names depend on them.

How to reproduce it

Build one evidence table for the whole batch before reading anything: disassembly per function, direct and indirect call targets with import names, referenced strings, and an exact call-target scan for callers. Read short functions fully and heads plus tails of large float ones. Cross-check vtable layouts, verified rewrite doc comments and lane vocabulary precedent before finalising names.

What was confusing or went wrong

Caller attribution by nearest known symbol below the call site produced several bogus results inside dense unnamed regions; exact call-target matches are trustworthy but the attributed caller names are hints only. One log timestamp was written from memory instead of the machine clock and had to be corrected.

entry.title: Naming a run of particle-effect functions
entry.summary: One hundred and fifty consecutive functions turned out to be the particle effects system, not streaming as labelled, and nearly all of them could be named from their vtables, strings and neighbours.
entry.content:
One hundred and fifty consecutive functions turned out to be the particle effects system, not streaming as labelled, and nearly all of them could be named from their vtables, strings and neighbours.

What was asked

Propose a descriptive name for each of 150 consecutive unnamed functions, with a confidence grade, working only from the executable file.

What was found

Verified The whole range belongs to the particle effects system: effect rules, timelines, keyframes, property lists, models, triggers, render state and spawn domains.

Verified Every class follows the same three-part idiom: a one-time descriptor builder referencing a type name string, a small factory allocating the class-sized block, and a final vtable slot returning the descriptor. A shared table callback reaches that slot through a virtual call, which confirms what the slot does.

Verified The range holds a complete introsort over effect instances ordered by a sort key: quicksort with a depth limit, a heap sort fallback, and a guarded insertion pass for the first entries followed by an unguarded one. The unguarded pass has no lower-bound check, which is what proves the split.

Inferred Four near-identical routines are keyframe samplers for different channel modes behind one bitmask-gated dispatcher; three produce four floats and one produces a single float.

What was decided or recommended

One hundred and forty-four functions were named and six were left empty where the meaning could not be determined, including one getter shared by dozens of unrelated classes. The next naming lane on nearby code should reuse the descriptor idiom above: any tiny routine returning a class global next to a type-name string is almost certainly the descriptor getter, and any routine taking an instance plus a time value near the timeline code is a track updater.

How to reproduce it

Read code through the mapped image rather than the raw file, rebuild the vtable runs from the read-only data section, and recover class names from the runtime type records stored just above each table. Then group functions by the class that references them before reading any bodies.

What was confusing or went wrong

All of the small XML, file and allocator helpers decode as garbage from the file on disk because that code range is encrypted at rest, so their roles had to be inferred from calling patterns and string arguments instead of read directly. The inventory subsystem labels for the range were also wrong, which cost an early detour before the type records settled the question.

entry.title: Production lane: when the import lookup misses and the loop never ends
entry.summary: A production batch of seven network functions verified six and deferred one, and the two interesting problems were both checker gaps with workarounds: an import-slot lookup that fails on a valid import, and a worker thread loop whose body cannot run in the checker at all.
entry.content:
A production batch of seven network functions verified six and deferred one, and the two interesting problems were both checker gaps with workarounds: an import-slot lookup that fails on a valid import, and a worker thread loop whose body cannot run in the checker at all.

What was asked

Rewrite seven neighbouring network functions in Rust and prove each identical to the original with the version four checker, or defer with a stated reason.

What was found

Verified Six functions passed twelve hundred trials each with their deliberately wrong versions caught, covering timer ticks, constructors, a send path and a session builder.

Verified The checker's import-slot lookup reported a network send import as missing even though the import exists with a valid table, so both sides faulted on send trials. Planting the stub address into the slot through the contract's global seeding, the documented data-table interception path, fixed it with no worker change.

Verified The largest function is a worker thread loop that spins until a shutdown flag is set, and nothing in its body writes the flag, so a clear flag hangs the trial and a set flag runs only the prologue and epilogue. The exit path was proven over twelve hundred trials, and a wrong version touching only the body passed every trial, which is what forced the deferral rather than a partial verify.

Verified Smaller traps, each confirmed by a failing then passing run: every address the original forms as a value must be relocated in the rewrite, not just dereferenced globals; two same-length trial cycles can lock a branch onto one outcome; argument order follows push order with the last push first; an early exit can return a leftover arithmetic value rather than the obvious one.

What was decided or recommended

Lanes hitting the import lookup failure should plant the stub into the slot and say so, instead of stopping. Worker loops gated on a fixed flag should be deferred with an exit-path proof and a body wrong version that demonstrates the gap, following this lane's retry kit. Trial-cycle lengths for gates and data should differ so every branch combination occurs.

How to reproduce it

Run the lane's contracts with the stock checker and worker: the send contract passes only with the planted slot, and the worker-loop contract passes its exit proof while the body wrong version passes too. The lane report lists the exact trial patterns that cover every branch of each function.

What was confusing or went wrong

Built rewrite libraries stayed locked against replacement for over twenty minutes with no process holding them, so each build used a fresh library name. One function's listed size cut off its last ten bytes including the return, which cost a careful tail decode before the contract could patch the cookie check.

entry.title: Naming a sky-to-session batch: descriptors beat disassembly
entry.summary: One hundred thirty-two of one hundred fifty functions got names, and the best evidence never came from reading instructions: class descriptors, message registration blocks, and verified neighbours named whole families at once.
entry.content:
One hundred thirty-two of one hundred fifty functions got names, and the best evidence never came from reading instructions: class descriptors, message registration blocks, and verified neighbours named whole families at once.

What was asked

Propose names for a batch of one hundred fifty consecutive unnamed functions spanning sky rendering and multiplayer session code, with a confidence per name.

What was found

Verified Three registration patterns named most of the batch. Sky classes each have a lazy descriptor builder (name, size, factory, member offsets) plus a tiny virtual getter returning its global, so sizes and factories check in both directions. Session message pack/parse wrappers each point at a descriptor global that registration code fills with a numeric id and a message name, which named all nineteen wrappers and exposed four pack/parse twin pairs sharing one descriptor. Session event getters return small type ids whose writes were found.

Verified Verified rewrites of neighbouring functions mapped every texture setter and loader to its texture name through the names pushed at each call site, cross-checked against slot offsets.

Verified Two listed entries are not functions: one opens with another function switch stubs, the other is a jump table; and one listed size spans five real functions.

What was decided or recommended

Inferred The next naming lane covering encrypted-code callers should scan for writes to the callee descriptor globals first: the id plus name string beside each write identifies the message without touching the encrypted bytes. Pack versus parse direction was inferred from argument shapes and caller roles and should be treated as medium confidence.

How to reproduce it

Build a mapped-image reader over the executable, dump each function callees and string references, resolve vtable slots through the merged symbols, scan the code section for direct callers, then scan for absolute writes to each descriptor global and read the id and name beside each hit.

What was confusing or went wrong

An early evidence script zipped deduplicated call lists against deduplicated name lists separately, misattributing names to the wrong call targets; pairing address and name before deduplicating fixed it. The inventory subsystem labels were wrong for two thirds of the batch, and the encrypted code range made several callees unreadable, which cost the most time before the descriptor workaround.

entry.title: Naming a mixed batch: session code, particles and water shaders
entry.summary: One hundred fifty consecutive unnamed functions turned out to be four subsystems, and the reliable signals were the callers, not the functions themselves: a dispatch table in the session handler named ten identical predicates, and vtable slots plus the class catalog named the render constructors.
entry.content:
One hundred fifty consecutive unnamed functions turned out to be four subsystems, and the reliable signals were the callers, not the functions themselves: a dispatch table in the session handler named ten identical predicates, and vtable slots plus the class catalog named the render constructors.

What was asked

Propose a descriptive name and confidence for each of 150 consecutive unnamed game functions, working out what the group is about first, then naming each function from strings, imports, known callers, classes and data flow.

What was found

Verified The batch splits into session management, a message codec layer, the particle system and water procedural textures. Twelve names are high confidence, ninety-one medium, and forty-seven were left empty.

Verified Ten near-identical session predicates each guard one branch of the session handler; the branch context (join, drop, presence flags, filter and others) distinguishes them.

Verified The render half follows strict vtable patterns: constructor, deleting destructor, a shared-data getter, a param-hash cache step and a param bind step per shader class.

Inferred The message codec functions cannot be distinguished until the small transport primitives they all call get names; the wrappers around encrypted-range helpers likewise stay unnamed.

What was decided or recommended

Named 103 functions and left 47 empty rather than invent wording. The next naming lane on codec code should name the shared primitives first, and any lane near render code should check the class structure catalog before reading disassembly.

How to reproduce it

Build one evidence table per function (string references, imports, named callees, caller scan, vtable pointer scan), dump the calling handler skeleton to place each predicate in its branch, dump near-identical callee heads side by side to find the single differing parameter, and confirm constructors against the class catalog vtable entries.

What was confusing or went wrong

A byte string that reads as a compression error message is compared as a single flag byte in one function, so the apparent string reference is partly coincidental. Several apparent string hits on vtable addresses are garbage reads of vtable bytes. Both now get verified against the referencing instruction before use.

entry.title: Naming a mixed batch: particles, fragments, joints and sky shaders
entry.summary: A batch of one hundred and fifty consecutive unnamed functions turned out to span four areas: the particle effect system, fragment physics, joint solving, and sky and shader code. One hundred and thirty-seven received names, nineteen at high confidence and the rest at medium; thirteen were left unnamed where the evidence ran out.
entry.content:
A batch of one hundred and fifty consecutive unnamed functions turned out to span four areas: the particle effect system, fragment physics, joint solving, and sky and shader code. One hundred and thirty-seven received names, nineteen at high confidence and the rest at medium; thirteen were left unnamed where the evidence ran out.

What was asked

Propose a descriptive name for each function in the batch, with a confidence level and one sentence of evidence, working out what the group is about before naming individuals.

What was found

Verified The batch splits into a particle block (effect pools, a quicksort/heapsort family sorting instances by distance, per-instance transform setters and the per-frame tick path), a fragment block (tuning singleton, a physics-update dispatcher running seven phases, joint builders, child lists and a small hash map), a three-function fragment-type parse and serialize group, and a shader tail (shader-fragment list handling, a sky-noise variable cache, a matrix transpose).

Verified The most useful signal was a scan of every direct call in the code section, resolving each caller against the merged, lane and verified name lists. It identified the sort family, the spawn and tick path, the physics dispatcher and the parse and serialize pair in one pass.

Verified A scan for vtable-pointer stores, checked against runtime type information, identified several constructors and a base destructor directly.

Verified Three inventory sizes were badly inflated: the real functions are tiny jump thunks, and everything past the jump is padding plus unrelated table entries. Evidence gathered past such a jump belongs to other functions.

Verified Four one-instruction virtual setters are linker-folded copies shared across dozens of unrelated classes, so the same bytes mean different things per class. They were left unnamed rather than misnamed.

What was decided or recommended

Functions were named for observed behaviour (what they allocate, copy, compute or dispatch to) with the class attached only where a vtable, constructor store or named caller anchored it. The next naming lane should run the caller scan first, distrust caller names from the encrypted region, decode each function for real before trusting its listed size, and check tiny virtuals for cross-class sharing before naming them.

How to reproduce it

Read the executable through mapped addresses, disassemble each batch entry, scan the code section for direct calls to batch addresses and resolve the callers against the merged symbols, lane names and verified index, scan batch bodies for vtable-pointer stores and confirm targets through runtime type information, then read the short functions fully and the heads of the large ones. The lane scratch folder keeps the scripts used.

What was confusing or went wrong

An early pass misresolved a plain code call as a cryptography import and briefly suggested the fragment relocate helper used encryption; checking the target showed a normal relocation applier. String harvesting initially included the code section, which decodes as garbage pseudo-strings; only data-section references were used after that. Several callees sit in the encrypted region and cannot be read, which caps a number of names at medium.

entry.title: A stat function passes its caller's leftover register to its clamp check
entry.summary: One statistic routine in the network batch passes its caller's saved register contents, not the sum it just computed, as the second argument to its clamp-check helper. The routine still clamps correctly, because it reloads the sum from its spill slot afterwards. The finding is verified by differential testing: a rewrite that passed the sum failed every trial that reached the call, and passing the entry register value instead passes all trials.
entry.content:
One statistic routine in the network batch passes its caller's saved register contents, not the sum it just computed, as the second argument to its clamp-check helper. The routine still clamps correctly, because it reloads the sum from its spill slot afterwards. The finding is verified by differential testing: a rewrite that passed the sum failed every trial that reached the call, and passing the entry register value instead passes all trials.

What was asked

Rewrite a batch of seven statistic-subsystem functions in Rust and prove each rewrite behaves identically to the original with the project checker, which runs both sides from identical starting state and compares return values, memory writes, outgoing calls and faults.

What was found

Verified The statistic add routine spills its new total four bytes past the helper's argument slot, so the helper reads the caller's entry register value still sitting in the register-save slot. Reproducing the trial inputs showed the helper receiving the entry register value exactly, and no input float added to the trial amount could produce the observed value any other way.

Verified A sibling routine in the same batch reads its own return address off the stack and uses it as an evolving exclusive-or key for stored bytes. That behaviour cannot be reproduced by a rewrite, so the function was deferred with the reason recorded.

Verified A two-switch dispatcher in the batch has only eleven live key mappings out of several hundred table entries; the rest return immediately. A ratio-report path in it is guarded by two ordered comparisons that proceed on unordered (not-a-number) inputs rather than skipping.

What was decided or recommended

The rewrites take the leftover register value and the caller-stack word as explicit extra parameters fed with the same per-trial values, keeping the comparison exact with no narrowing. The return-address keyed function is deferred as unimplementable. Later lanes should check spill-slot arithmetic against argument-slot positions whenever a helper call immediately follows a spill: two functions in this batch read a different slot than a quick reading suggests.

How to reproduce it

Disassemble the statistic add routine and trace the stack offsets of the spill store and the helper call: the store lands one word above the slot the helper reads. Then run the checker contract for the function with a rewrite that passes the computed sum: every trial that reaches the helper call fails on that argument, showing the entry register value instead.

What was confusing or went wrong

The first probe failures looked paradoxical: the helper received a tiny value while the recorded total was large, which no arithmetic could explain. The paradox resolved only after re-deriving every stack offset from the entry pushes. A second function initially failed the same way: its low-byte test reads one word above its own argument, which is caller stack, not the argument. Both cases were the same lesson: trust the offsets, not the apparent intent.

entry.title: A wrong rewrite passed, and it should not have
entry.summary: A deliberately wrong rewrite that stored a table row at the wrong index passed its proof contract on every trial, which exposed a soundness hole in the checker's comparison of written global values: only the start of each watched region is recorded, never the address of each write.
entry.content:
A deliberately wrong rewrite that stored a table row at the wrong index passed its proof contract on every trial, which exposed a soundness hole in the checker's comparison of written global values: only the start of each watched region is recorded, never the address of each write.

What was asked

Rewrite a batch of six network-subsystem functions in Rust and prove each one identical to the original with the project's checker, giving every function its own deliberately wrong version that must fail the same proof.

What was found

Verified Five of the six functions were verified at 1200 trials each with their wrong versions caught. The sixth was deferred on time with a passing first stage and a written plan for the rest.

Verified One wrong version changed a table scan from strict to non-strict comparison, so tied rows resolved to the last index instead of the first. It passed every trial. The cause is in the checker's write log: for each changed word it records the watched region's base address instead of the word's own address, so identical values stored at different offsets inside one region compare equal. The heap and stack comparisons both use exact offsets, which is why only globals are affected.

Verified Declaring one watched region per word restores exact comparison: the same wrong version then fails immediately, showing the two differing addresses. All of this lane's globals contracts were rewritten that way.

Inferred Earlier verdicts that watch multi-word regions are weaker than they look wherever a rewrite could misplace a store without changing the stored values or their order. Offset errors that reorder differently-valued writes were always caught.

What was decided or recommended

The defect was reported to the coordinator with a reproducer (the wrong version plus a forced-tie contract) and a suggested one-line fix. Until the checker is fixed, lanes should declare single-word watched regions. A re-run sweep of earlier multi-word-region verdicts was recommended.

How to reproduce it

Take any verified function that stores the same values at an index chosen by the trial, write a wrong version that picks a different index with equal values in the same order, and run it against a contract with one wide watched region: it passes. Split the region into one word each and it fails.

What was confusing or went wrong

The escaping wrong version looked impossible for a while: the tie trials demonstrably ran, the comparison code looked sound at first glance, and the heap behaviour was correct, which kept pointing suspicion at the contract instead of the checker. Printing both sides' raw write logs side by side showed identical entries for different addresses and ended the hunt. Two smaller environment snags cost a few minutes each: a rewrite library stays locked after a worker uses it, so each rebuild went under a new file name, and the driver overwrites the lane results file, so all driver output went to a separate folder.

entry.title: Naming fragments and particle effects: field readers fall out of one registration table
entry.summary: A batch of one hundred and fifty consecutive unnamed functions turned out to be three subsystems: fragment instances and their streaming, a type-erased container with eight holder types, and the particle effect manager. One hundred and forty-four got names; the rest stayed empty where the evidence ran out.
entry.content:
A batch of one hundred and fifty consecutive unnamed functions turned out to be three subsystems: fragment instances and their streaming, a type-erased container with eight holder types, and the particle effect manager. One hundred and forty-four got names; the rest stayed empty where the evidence ran out.

What was asked

Propose a descriptive project-style name for each function in the batch, with a confidence level and one sentence of evidence, working from strings, imports, known callers, virtual tables and behaviour.

What was found

Verified The fragment archetype registers its fields through one function that pairs each field name string with a reader callback. Every reader in the batch is referenced exactly once from inside that function, so each reader maps to its field name with certainty: twenty-two readers covering class, child, group, damage and rope flags, cache sizes, centre-of-gravity offsets, six damping vectors, self-collision data, asset id and collision events.

Verified The matching writer virtual serialises the same fields by value, with tab characters after each field name, which pins down the text format.

Verified The type-erased container resolves cleanly: each holder type has a distinct virtual table, each assignment routine sets one of those same tables, and the type-info getter returns a descriptor holding the mangled type name. Eight assignment routines, eight clone routines and eight type getters, all matched.

Verified The particle manager has symmetric load and remove routines over five tables (rule banks, emit rules, effect rules, models, textures), plus spawn, depth sort, three update phases and three pools. Its create and destroy routines mirror each other through the same globals.

Verified One heavily referenced getter is called from over a hundred sites and selects between the streamed fragment type and a stub. It is the single most connected function in the batch.

What was decided or recommended

  • Names follow the field strings and table roles found above; wording-only guesses stay at medium confidence and six functions stay unnamed.
  • A memory-copy routine carries a script-native name from an earlier lane and should be renamed; nearby constructor and destructor labels on the fragment archetype look swapped and need review.
  • Two inventory sizes are wrong: one function extends past its listed size into padding, and one entry overlaps the two functions after it. Later lanes should distrust sizes and re-derive them from control flow.
  • Caller attribution by nearest known function below fails badly in sparsely named regions, with offsets of several kilobytes. Attributions that far away should be treated as unknown.

How to reproduce it

Read code through the mapped image only, never the raw file at a mapped address. Build one evidence table for the whole batch first: per-function calls resolved against the merged names, referenced strings, import calls, caller sites from a byte-level scan for direct calls, and virtual table references from data scans. Verify the mapping by decoding one known function end to end, then decode the short and unclear functions fully and read the raw virtual tables to confirm slot numbers.

What was confusing or went wrong

Two dozen functions had no direct callers and no table references, which first looked like dead code; they turned out to be callbacks passed as immediate arguments, found only by scanning for their immediate values. One pool routine is reached by a jump thunk, which a call-only scan also misses. Several callees sit in the encrypted code region and decode as garbage, so behaviour there had to come from callers and siblings instead. An early caller table misattributed one helper to a destructor; rechecking the raw call sites fixed it.

entry.title: Naming batch forty: task slot roles, shared code traps, and a misnamed constructor
entry.summary: One hundred and fifty consecutive functions got names, one hundred and forty five of them with useful confidence, and the batch paid for itself three times over: the three sub-task slots shared by every complex task now have project-backed meanings, five inventory sizes were caught overrunning their real functions, and a production-lane constructor name was shown to be wrong.
entry.content:
One hundred and fifty consecutive functions got names, one hundred and forty five of them with useful confidence, and the batch paid for itself three times over: the three sub-task slots shared by every complex task now have project-backed meanings, five inventory sizes were caught overrunning their real functions, and a production-lane constructor name was shown to be wrong.

What was asked

Name one hundred and fifty consecutive unnamed functions, mostly from the same source files: medic and fire tasks, cop and arrest tasks, ped data, render phases, interface markup parsing, radar blips, and the dispatch order system. Names only, no rewrites, each with a confidence and one sentence of evidence.

What was found

Verified The last three slots of every complex task form a first, next and control trio: the first-slot body never touches the current sub task and builds the initial one, the next-slot body reads the current sub task and picks the follow up, and the control-slot body drives the current sub task or just hands it back. This held for every complex class in the batch that overrides more than one of them, and two wander cases delegate to the base implementation outright.

Verified The current sub task lives eight bytes into the task object. That contradicts the drafted layout, which calls that field flags, so one of the two needs correcting.

Verified Five inventory sizes run past the real end of their functions, in one case deep into later batch entries, so a plain linear read invents calls that belong to neighbouring code. The affected entries are listed in the lane report for fixing.

Verified A constructor a production lane named as audio code is really a simple-task constructor: it calls the task base constructor and is used to build wander sub tasks. It needs a new name.

Inferred The radar blip names, the interface markup attribute pipeline and a family of hash tables form one data system: blip names are registered into a global table, config blocks are tokenised into attributes, and the attributes are applied to the same render state the markup code initialises.

Unknown Several read-only float constants decode as denormal numbers near zero while their bit patterns look like code addresses. One task slot that returns such a value was left unnamed because its meaning could not be established.

What was decided or recommended

  • Record the first, next and control slot roles in a shared slot table so future naming lanes stop re-deriving them.
  • Fix the five overrunning sizes and re-check anything whose evidence came from a linear sweep past an early return.
  • Adjudicate the two layout disputes (sub task pointer versus flags, pointer versus flag bit) and rename the misnamed constructor.
  • Keep three reliable shapes on file: pool allocation plus constructor means clone, an indirect call through the sub task means a type query, and a jump table full of constructors means a factory keyed by type id.

How to reproduce it

Open the lane scratch folder for this batch and read the evidence table, the annotated disassembly and the names file. Re-derive the trio by comparing which sub-task slots read the field eight bytes into the object and which only allocate. Re-check each overrun by decoding from the entry until the first return or tail jump and comparing the length with the inventory size.

What was confusing or went wrong

The batch list had to be re-read twice: two addresses remembered from the evidence output turned out not to be in the batch at all, and the near-identical layout of neighbouring task code makes this easy. Trust the batch file, not memory. The security-cookie slot also decodes as a plausible-looking string fragment and wasted a few minutes before it was recognised for what it is.

entry.title: Naming lane: browser layout, radar blips and task clones
entry.summary: One hundred fifty consecutive functions came apart into clean groups: an in-game web browser with stylesheet and table layout code, a radar and blip system with a tidy accessor family, viewport render methods, vehicle and ped factories, and task clone and destructor methods. 145 are named, 90 with high confidence.
entry.content:

What was asked

Propose a descriptive name for each of 150 consecutive unnamed functions, working out what the group is about first, with a confidence grade and one sentence of evidence each.

What was found

Verified The largest group is the in-game web browser: element parsing, style matching with hover rules, box layout, text measurement, and a full table section with column measurement, width distribution and row layout.

Verified The radar group is a family of tiny accessors over one blip record table, plus four draw routines selected by blip type from a per-frame update, and dedicated centre and north blips.

Verified Five viewport classes each override the same three methods: refresh, release and render, where render builds and attaches render phases. Four task slot-1 methods are clones and two slot-6 methods return urgency constants, confirmed by matching verified rewrites of the same slots.

Verified Three functions in the range are not in the inventory: a fifth blip draw routine, a radar update gate, and a small destructor-like function. Two listed sizes overlap their neighbours.

What was decided or recommended

Names follow the existing project vocabulary for the same slots and structures, so later lanes can treat equal slots as equal methods. The unlisted functions and wrong sizes were reported for the inventory keepers. Five tiny virtual methods whose purpose nothing reveals were left unnamed rather than guessed.

How to reproduce it

Disassemble each function from the mapped image, collect its string references, called imports and named callees, and check claimed constructors and clones by the vtable address they stamp against the recovered class table list. Merged names from other lanes need a trust check first: one low-confidence native mapping turned out to be a player-position helper, and far-away caller attributions collapse into the nearest known symbol.

What was confusing or went wrong

Indexing the mapped executable image by file offset instead of address produced convincing but fake strings until a cross-check caught it, and the whole evidence table had to be rebuilt. A generic array allocator contains a resource-loading path that cannot be resolved without running the game, so it is named for its observable behaviour only.
